title: The Destruction of the Pocket
subtitle: The defeat of the Soviet Southwestern Front
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: III — The Battle for Strategic Objectives
summary: The destruction of the principal Soviet grouping east of Kiev produced fragmented resistance, escape attempts and mass captivity. Forces outside the pocket continued fighting while German commanders prepared further operations.
body:
A battle ending in different places

By 26 September 1941, the German commands could describe the great encirclement east of Kiev as a completed victory. The principal bodies of the Soviet Southwestern Front had been broken into separate groups, their headquarters dispersed or destroyed, and enormous numbers of men taken prisoner. Yet the date describes the end of a major operation more satisfactorily than it describes the experience of everyone caught within it. A soldier seeking a way through a village, a wounded man awaiting transport and a prisoner being marched west did not enter a common state of peace when the battle disappeared from the operational agenda. The destruction of the armies thus opened into captivity, dispersal and attempts at escape. German control over prisoners and occupied communities would determine consequences that the operational declaration of victory could not settle.[1][2]

The decisive change since 16 September was the loss of the ability to act together. Closing the German pincers had interrupted routes. Subsequent attacks divided the space inside them, captured crossings and deprived Soviet formations of the means to coordinate their efforts. The fall of Kiev on 19 September removed the city from Soviet control, but it neither produced a simultaneous surrender farther east nor released every German formation for its next operation. Reducing the pocket required another sequence of movements, engagements and decisions.

The distinction matters when assessing the German achievement. An encirclement was valuable because it could destroy an enemy force that might otherwise retreat and fight again. That destruction required time, ammunition and troops. A mobile division holding a road against a breakout could not use the same battalions to advance toward a distant objective. Infantry advancing into the pocket had to maintain its own connections while taking responsibility for prisoners and captured equipment. The apparent simplicity of a closed line on a campaign map concealed several different kinds of work, each competing for resources.

For the Soviet side, the collapse of command magnified material inferiority. Men who still possessed weapons might lack ammunition for prolonged resistance, a reliable route east or knowledge of where neighbouring formations stood. Their continued fighting demonstrates that the defeat cannot be reduced to an absence of courage. It also cannot reverse the operational result. An army survives as an army through communications, supply and coordinated movement as well as through the willingness of individuals to resist. Around Kiev, those connecting institutions were being destroyed faster than they could be restored.

The ring becomes a series of smaller battles

The original encirclement contained the 5th, 21st, 26th and 37th Armies, or substantial portions of them, together with other troops and rear services. They had entered the crisis from different positions. The 37th Army had been defending Kiev; the 5th and 21st were associated with the threatened northern sector; the 26th held positions farther south. A withdrawal toward the east therefore began from several fronts and required convergence on roads and crossings already threatened by German mobile formations. It was never a single column marching toward one open gate.[3]

On the German side, Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group continued to face in two directions. Its inner front helped contain the trapped troops; its outer front resisted Soviet forces still operating beyond the pocket. In his postwar study for the U.S. Army, Guderian described the 3rd Panzer Division pushing toward Piryatin and the SS Division Das Reich taking Priluki. These movements tightened the northeastern part of the encirclement by taking places through which Soviet troops might otherwise move. Their significance lay in the roads and communications they controlled, rather than in the addition of two names to a list of captured towns.[2]

The 25th Motorised Infantry Division, approaching from Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group, helped establish the connection with the northern forces and faced Soviet attempts to break through farther south. The infantry armies pressed from the wider perimeter: Weichs’s 2nd Army from the northern side and Reichenau’s 6th Army from the west, while the southern German grouping secured the approaches opened from the Kremenchuk bridgehead. The relationship between the advancing infantry and the mobile formations was crucial. Infantry pressure compressed the Soviet groups; mobile forces could intercept their movement toward the eastern exits. Neither function alone explains the result.[2][1]

Movement within the pocket became increasingly difficult because the same streams and rivers crossed during the advance now constrained escape. The Udai and Sula systems divided routes into a limited number of usable passages. A formation reaching a crossing could find another group already there, German troops beyond it or no information about the road ahead. Such conditions favoured smaller parties that could abandon vehicles, but they imposed severe disadvantages on artillery, medical units and transport columns. Saving people and saving an organised army were becoming different problems.

German pressure also separated Soviet commanders from the troops they were meant to direct. The published Soviet command conversations record the loss of communications with army headquarters before the fighting ended. On 19 September, higher headquarters were still trying to establish what had happened to the 5th Army after receiving an intercepted appeal from the Piryatin area. A missing report was not proof that a formation had surrendered; it was evidence that the command system could no longer dependably locate and employ it. The resulting uncertainty made a coordinated breakout progressively less achievable.[4]

Headquarters on the road

The Southwestern Front headquarters itself became part of the retreat. Kirponos and his staff could no longer direct the battle from a secure centre connected to the armies by dependable communications. The headquarters column had to move through the same contested countryside as the troops whose movements it was attempting to organise. Its escorts and vehicles offered some protection and mobility, but the concentration also made it a target. The defeat of a headquarters in these circumstances was both a human disaster and the destruction of an institution containing knowledge, records and established working relationships.

On 20 September, Kirponos was killed in fighting near the Shumeikove grove by Driukivshchyna, southwest of Lokhvytsia. The Ukrainian academic biographical reference gives that date and records his death in combat; its account of the wider operation places the destruction of the combined front and 5th Army headquarters column across 20–22 September. These are compatible descriptions of an individual death and a longer sequence of fighting. They should not be compressed into a claim that every senior officer died at the same moment. Chief of staff Vasilii Tupikov and military council member Mikhail Burmistenko also died in the destruction of the command group, while the wounded 5th Army commander, Mikhail Potapov, became a prisoner.[5][3]

The loss of the staff was especially damaging because it removed people capable of reconnecting scattered formations. A surviving commander could assemble men locally, but might not know where to find another army’s remnants or where friendly forces beyond the ring could assist. The destruction of radio equipment, codes and transport further narrowed what authority could accomplish. The personal rank of a general remained recognizable; the practical means of exercising command could disappear. That distinction helps explain why survival by individual officers did not mean the Southwestern Front had escaped intact.

The published Soviet conversations also show the limits of help from outside. On 20 September, headquarters discussed delivering fuel and ammunition by air to the encircled troops and using combat aircraft to supplement scarce transport capacity. These exchanges establish an effort to assist, not a completed resupply operation. Even successful drops could support only those recipients who could find and distribute the supplies. Fuel reaching one group would not open a road for another; ammunition could prolong a local defence without restoring a front-wide plan. The supply problem had become inseparable from the destruction of communications.[4]

Breakout attempts consequently had different outcomes at different scales. A party reaching Soviet lines could preserve trained men and valuable information. A larger formation might force a temporary passage yet lose cohesion during the movement beyond it. Others found their route blocked and fought until their capacity to continue was exhausted. Recognising those differences gives the surviving troops their due without confusing escape with an operational rescue. The central fact remained that the Soviet command could no longer extract the encircled armies as functioning formations.

The outer front still demands fuel

While the trapped forces were being reduced, Soviet attacks outside the encirclement continued to occupy German troops. Guderian’s account places a serious attack near his headquarters at Romny on 18 September, involving Soviet cavalry and tanks. German infantry, antiaircraft weapons employed against ground targets, armour and air support were brought into the response. The episode demonstrates how close an apparent victory could remain to an active threat. A headquarters positioned to control the encirclement was still vulnerable to enemy forces that had never entered it.[2]

On 19 September, Guderian reported that a shortage of fuel restricted the forces he could move eastward: only small elements of Das Reich and the 4th Panzer Division could initially be shifted. The following day, movements from Romny toward Nedryhailiv and from the Putivl area toward Vorozhba sought to push the outer front away from the encirclement. These were efforts to improve security and freedom of movement, not evidence that the Soviet armies outside the pocket had ceased to matter. The Germans had to spend fuel to obtain the space within which they could finish their victory.[2]

Soviet records provide a useful view from the opposite side of this outer battle. The command conversation of 20 September placed Belov’s 9th and 5th Cavalry Divisions east and southeast of Romny after difficult fighting on the previous day. It also reported the 1st Tank Brigade unloading at Lebedyn and concentrating farther west, while the 129th Tank Brigade was gathering closer to Romny. This was a force being assembled through distinct stages, with cavalry already fighting while additional armour arrived by rail. The report explicitly lacked the latest positions of some units. It consequently supports an account of continuing pressure and reinforcement, rather than a claim that every formation was simultaneously ready to attack. The same sequence explains why a German commander might face a serious local threat without facing a fully coordinated Soviet relief offensive. [4]

The fighting around Glukhov supplied another reminder. Soviet attacks threatened German communications, and the 17th Panzer Division was employed in relieving the endangered garrison on 23 September. In a simplified account, the mobile formations join, the pocket surrenders and the tanks proceed to their next objective. The actual sequence included detachments sent outward, units held back by shortages and formations diverted to restore connections. These demands explain why the operational value of a division could not be measured only by whether its headquarters still appeared on the order of battle.[2]

German material weakness should therefore be dated and defined. The U.S. Army’s study of the campaign reports that on 4 September only 47 percent of the tanks on the Eastern Front were operational, with another 23 percent in repair and 30 percent disabled. Those figures describe the theatre at an earlier date; they are not a measured inventory of the divisions around Kiev on 26 September. Their value is to establish the deteriorating equipment position in which the final battle developed. A repaired tank could return to service, while a vehicle still counted in a unit’s holdings might be unavailable for its next movement.[6]

Infantry victory carried its own burden. Marching troops needed food and ammunition, horses needed fodder, and wounded men needed transport back through roads also used for supply. Captured guns and vehicles had to be identified, collected and moved before they became useful resources. Prisoners required guards and provisions. The German command could choose to subordinate those needs to preparation for another offensive, but that choice did not abolish them. In the case of prisoners, the decisions made about supply and movement would become matters of life and death.

Counting a destroyed front

The familiar German claim of 665,000 prisoners expresses the scale of the Kiev victory, but it is not a simple census of men surrendering in one place on 26 September. It was a claim associated with the completed operation. The U.S. Army’s later synthesis places it alongside a Soviet published figure of 677,085 men in the Southwestern Front at the beginning of the battle and 150,541 at its end. These numbers belong to different accounting systems. Subtracting the latter two does not produce a verified prisoner total, because losses, transfers, arrivals, wounded personnel and the boundaries of the reporting period affect the comparison.[1]

Historian Dieter Pohl identifies a broader difficulty in reconciling German capture statistics with Soviet military losses. German prisoner categories could include people outside the Red Army’s regular strength returns, including other uniformed personnel and civilians mobilised for construction or militia service. Soviet reporting also suffered from the collapse of formations and incomplete records. Pohl therefore treats the discrepancy as an unresolved historical accounting problem rather than a reason to accept either series automatically. His discussion makes the figure of roughly 660,000 a German claim requiring definition, not a substitute for tracing who was actually captured.[7]

Equipment claims require the same care. A gun found abandoned, a tank knocked out and a vehicle subsequently repaired describe different events. German collection reports were measuring the apparent destruction of enemy resources; Soviet loss returns addressed changes within their own organisations. Neither category alone measures how much additional fighting power the German army acquired. A captured weapon without compatible ammunition, trained users or transport might remain a trophy rather than an immediately useful asset. Operational success and usable replenishment were related, but they were not identical.

These distinctions also affect how losses are remembered. A man missing from his unit might later appear in a camp record, return after escape or remain unaccounted for. His family’s uncertainty could persist long after headquarters had classified the formation as destroyed. Administrative closure and personal knowledge followed different timetables.

There is no need to resolve every statistical discrepancy before recognising the magnitude of the Soviet defeat. Several armies had lost their capacity to fight as organised bodies, major command staffs had been destroyed and a large territory had become exposed to further German operations. That conclusion is supported by the movements and institutional collapse described in the records. It does not depend upon presenting a contested total with an unwarranted appearance of precision. The strongest interpretation is the one that can explain what the numbers measure as well as repeat them.

The road into captivity

Capture changed a soldier’s vulnerability without necessarily improving his physical condition. Exhaustion, wounds and hunger acquired during the fighting accompanied him into German custody. Men separated from their units also lost the ordinary mechanisms through which an army might feed them, evacuate them or record their location. German military authorities now controlled their movement and access to supplies. The question of what happened to prisoners therefore belongs inside the history of the victory, rather than in a separate humanitarian appendix added after the military narrative ends.

Pohl distinguishes army collection points, transit camps known as Dulags, and more permanent camps called Stalags. Transfer between them did not remove military responsibility: even camps inside the civilian Reichskommissariat Ukraine remained under Wehrmacht supervision. This institutional chain connected the troops taking prisoners with the authorities responsible for their longer confinement.[7]

The German high command had already defined Soviet captivity in ideological terms. Regulations of 8 September treated Red Army prisoners as bearers of Bolshevism and authorized exceptional severity. They provided for the separation of prisoners classified as politically undesirable and their transfer to Security Police and Security Service units. The military custody system and the security apparatus were connected by policy. A soldier who survived surrender could consequently face further selection and killing after leaving the battlefield.[8]

A warning read and rejected

On 15 September, Admiral Wilhelm Canaris sent Keitel a memorandum objecting to the treatment prescribed for Soviet prisoners. It warned that the instructions on the use of weapons could produce arbitrary killings and challenged the abandonment of established protections. Keitel’s response, written on the document on 23 September, endorsed the measures on ideological grounds. The exchange is preserved in the Nuremberg documentary record as EC-338. It is revealing because it establishes that objections existed within the German military apparatus while the Kiev pocket was being destroyed. The warning had reached the leadership. Keitel’s annotation shows him rejecting the protections invoked in the objection and sustaining the measures on the ideological grounds under which the war was being fought. Canaris’s intervention does not absolve the wider institution; it makes the decision at the top more clearly identifiable. The relevant distinction is between a warning that reached authority and an order that authority chose to sustain.[8]

The treatment of prisoners also exposes the limits of explaining every German failure through insufficient transport. A February 1942 memorandum from Rosenberg’s ministry, preserved as document 081-PS, described guards shooting prisoners unable to keep up on marches and camp commanders preventing civilians from providing food. It also reported a failure to provide shelter or even tools with which prisoners could dig protection. This was a later assessment of the wider system, not an eyewitness report of every Kiev column. Nevertheless, it demonstrates that deprivation involved deliberate restrictions as well as shortage. Food offered by civilians could be available and still be denied.[9]

The memorandum’s purpose was itself revealing. Rosenberg’s ministry wanted to improve recruitment, propaganda and the exploitation of labour. Its criticism did not amount to a rejection of German domination. By describing brutal treatment as a cause of Soviet resistance and a loss to Germany’s economy, it evaluated victims partly through their usefulness to the occupier. The document is powerful evidence against claims that the catastrophe was unknown within the regime, but its proposed remedy remained embedded in the regime’s purposes. Reading it critically requires attention both to the abuses it acknowledged and to the interests behind the complaint.[9]

A prisoner is more than a number

For civilians along the routes, the passage of prisoners brought the battle into another intimate setting. The later German memorandum describes inhabitants trying to feed captured men and being prevented from doing so. These interventions reveal a social world that the military classification of prisoners obscures. Someone behind the wire or on a guarded road might be a neighbour, a relative or simply a visibly hungry stranger. Assistance could be offered without any knowledge of his unit or political beliefs. German restrictions on that assistance turned the boundary of custody into a barrier between available civilian resources and people in urgent need.[9]

Volodymyr Davydov’s route west

The National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War preserves a biographical account of Volodymyr Davydov alongside his later testimony. Captured near Pereiaslav in late September 1941, he passed through places of confinement at Pereiaslav, Boryspil, Darnytsia, Kiev and Zhytomyr. He escaped from the Zhytomyr camp in late October and returned to Kiev. This sequence gives a human scale to the movement concealed inside a prisoner total: capture began a journey through several institutions and locations. The museum’s account does not establish his experience on every march or the exact day of each transfer, and those details should not be supplied imaginatively. His escape also warns against treating entry into captivity as an invariably final event. It was possible to survive and return, although the possibility did not reduce the danger faced by those who remained in German custody.[10]

Davydov’s itinerary also shows why a tally at one camp cannot be read as the entire population captured in the battle. Prisoners moved between collection points and camps; some escaped, some were released under particular policies, and others died before a later registration. A total for an institution at a particular date measures those present within its administrative reach. It cannot recover every person who passed through or disappeared along the way. The missing connections between military capture records and later camp records are part of the history, not an invitation to replace evidence with a single dramatic estimate.

Nor can the social consequences be confined to soldiers. The destruction of the Southwestern Front removed an armed barrier between civilians and occupation. Homes, farms and roads became resources for the victors, while people who helped fugitives or prisoners had to judge the new risks of doing so. Jewish soldiers and civilians faced the additional danger created by Nazi racial policy. The Soviet defeat and German decisions about treatment were separate causes operating together: military capture placed people in German power, and the occupiers determined what they would do with that power.[8]

What the victory made possible

By the conventional endpoint of 26 September, the German army had achieved an operational success of exceptional magnitude. It had prevented much of the Southwestern Front from withdrawing as an organised force, secured Kiev and opened possibilities for further movement in the south. Yet the cost of the operation remained present in worn vehicles, extended supply routes and formations requiring reorganisation. The U.S. Army campaign study records estimates that a proper refit would require several weeks. The approaching offensive timetable offered far less room than that estimate implied.[6]

The Soviet state had lost armies, but the forces beyond the pocket had continued to fight and the command was already attempting to rebuild a front. Germany therefore confronted another campaign rather than a completed war. For the people left behind, meanwhile, the change was immediate and lasting: the authority capable of ordering their movement, withholding their food or determining their survival had changed. The final chapter of this phase follows that connection between military success and occupation policy. It asks what the German victories had achieved strategically, and what their consolidation meant for the inhabitants of Kiev.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. Contemporary orders establish intentions, while reports contain the information, estimates and gaps known to their authors. Retrospective military accounts and testimony are identified and assessed alongside documentary evidence and scholarship. English paraphrases of Russian, Ukrainian and German texts are by the atlas unless a published translator is named. Archival references reproduced in published sources do not imply direct archival inspection. Events after the chapter date are dated explicitly. The companion map is a dated regional military reconstruction; its feature sources and precision notes distinguish reported positions from approximate connecting edges.
